Most books only show classic holography despite embossed holograms are the most.

Who are the main manufacturers of embossing machines, and who does the mastering?

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Is this really HoloM, revered as a god on the old Forum! Good to see you here.

But the down side is that much of the techniques involved in the mass reproduction of holograms via embossing are usually trade secrets and are rarely disclosed in refereed scientific journals or magazines. I should know, I worked at CFC/Northern Banknote, where I learned everything from spinning resist plates up to 42” (> 1 meter) square to shooting stereograms on a Multiplex machine that used a Texas Instruments DMD (is this the kind of digital holography you are thinking of? We used totally synthetic objects, sometimes combined with photos) to a dot matrix machine (another digital technology) to gratings, plus my best friend there was the plate maker and I learned how to do the nickel plating of the shims.

I am not reluctant to spill my guts on how to do all this, but there is not enough time for me to do so. The hardest part of the operation is to work out the details, which sometimes takes a lot of trial and error. Or just trying stuff, like Steve Provence turned us on to the fact that you don’t have to spin resist at hundreds or thousands of rpm’s! That’s just for the electronics dudes, it doesn’t matter how thick it is since you’re using the surface of it anyhow. This type of info you would probably find nowhere else but here, or possibly from a consultant, maybe. Or learn it yourself!

But that is not to say that there isn’t much literature out there, but it’s in the form of manufacturer’s brochures. Your first line of attack other than Googling is to check out the IHMA, International Holographic Manufacturers’ Association, as most of the machine makers and foil suppliers have bought into it.

Jeff Weil is more active in the field than anyone else here, and he could probably throw out more names than I could, but search for Peacock labs, for silvering chemistry, Ahead for dot matrix machines, and I am not so sure if that is what you mean by digital holography, but if you mean hologram patterns written directly onto photo resist, I think we used a place called Polski Holographie for e-beam holograms. Shipley was the photoresist we used for holograms, Townes was one fo the suppliers who spun plates, another Telic, not sure if that’s spelled correctly, BobH had mentioned to me some other names, hoepfully he’ll chime in.

Good luck and glad to see you’re still interested!

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **HoloM:** i read very much about holography yet, but i am wondering that the basic principles of digital generated embossed holograms are discussed very thin.Most books only show classic holography despite embossed holograms are the most.

> **HoloM:** I assume masters are mostly done on a photoresist, and then are metallized for embossing. Which companies do this?Which software is used?
 The main problem here are the words we use. They mean different things to different people in different fields. Embossed holograms are not digitally generated, if, "digitally" you mean some kind of software that outputs some kind of file. They are "digital" in that dot matrix machines are run by computers that run specific software, but the software runs the machine, it does not record the hologram. The lasers still record the hologram. To the best of my knowledge, there is no commercially available software that can make holograms. Companies and universities that make digital holograms write their own software.

In the holographic world, there are three basic kinds: embossed ("mass produced", "security" etc etc), HOE/DOE, classical display.

 In the first kind - "embossed" - a hologram is made by a variety of ways. This hologram is then electroformed to create a "shim", which is then embossed onto a substrate, or hot stamped onto foil. The actual embossing (or hot stamping) is usually not done by holographers, it's usually done by a separate company such as Novavision or Wavefront. Companies such as American Banknote (now JDSU) and Crown Roll leaf still do both the holography and the embossing (and many other things!), but this is not now any longer true. Nowadays, the actual holograms are made by individual companies or people such as Pacific Holography or (as Ed mentioned ) Jeff Weil.These holographers get their work from embossers who deal with the client and then "farm" out the holography. The holograms made by holographers or holographic companies are called "Glass Masters". After electroforming, they're called "Silver Masters". If you talk to an embosser, "master" means the product after silvering and electroforming. 

There s another form of "master" made by a technique called "lithography". In this technique, the pattern that a traditional hologram makes is etched directly onto the substrate to create a surface profile. There is software that calculates a lithographic pattern, which can then be impressed on a substrate (eg resist). These techniques are sometimes known as DOE's (Diffractive Optical Elements), because a diffraction pattern is calculated by the software for mostly technical optics. Another technique is known as "e-beam", where a beam of electrons etch into a substrate. There are machines and software used for controlling the electrons and making e-beam "holograms", but these are not traditional holograms. Some display embossed holograms use this lithographic-ebeam technique to produce masters which are then embossed. I believe De La Rue uses an e-beam method ( [http://www.delarue.com/ProductsSolution ... olutionsf/](http://www.delarue.com/ProductsSolutions/Holographics/BrandProtectionand/HologramSolutionsf/) ) E-beam technique are also lithographic, but to a much finer scale. 

On the other hand there are "digital" holograms that are made by software, but these are not embossed. The diffraction pattern of a hologram is calculated and the pattern is then etched directly onto the medium using a laser and lenses. Usually, the companies doing this have their own software. Zebra comes to mind. Zebra has some software on their site that you can use to make your own holograms, called "Zscape" ( [http://www.zebraimaging.com/](http://www.zebraimaging.com/) ). 

There are techniques are known as "CGH" (Computer Generated Holograms) and there is a lot of interest in them from academia. CGH is a mostly mathematical technique that calculates the hologram that would have been made by a conventional laser and then directly records the pattern onto a substrate. There is a great deal of academic interest in this technique but it's not usually seen by the public, as far as I know.

There are holograms made directly from CGI data, or data generated by equipment and then processed using CGI technique. On a display level, companies such as Liti ( [http://www.litiholographics.com/](http://www.litiholographics.com/) ) will take your video sequence, apply their own software and make a hologram. Holorad (formerly Voxel) takes CAT scan data generated by a CAT scan machine, procceses the raw CAT scan data into image data and then records a hologram composed of many individual CAT scan images. Holorad have their own propretry software to do this. We (Triple Take Holographics) have our own software that can also take imagery from any video sequence to make our "floating image" display ( [http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zgcKKgQPjuw](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zgcKKgQPjuw) ). The point is: any hologram company tha makes display holograms usually have written the software themselves, there's nothing off-the-shelf.

As for books, it depends on your technical level. A good series of books for the non-technical person are the "Holography Marketplace" by Ross Books ( [http://www.amazon.com/Holography-Market ... 0894960253](http://www.amazon.com/Holography-Marketplace-Alan-Rhody/dp/0894960253) ). These books, eight volumes in all,are a good source of undersatnding the different types of embossed holograms, the companies involved and the techniques. A more technical book is "Digital Diffractive Optics" ( [http://www.amazon.com/Digital-Diffracti ... 873&sr=1-1](http://www.amazon.com/Digital-Diffractive-Optics-Introduction-Technology/dp/0471984477/ref=sr_1_1?s=books&ie=UTF8&qid=1330648873&sr=1-1)).

As for papers, the SPIE Proceedings of the Practiacal Holography meetings are full of papers on CGH. The new one for this year's convention just came out ([http://spie.org/x648.html?product_id=897088](http://spie.org/x648.html?product_id=897088) ). At a (much!) higher technical level, look for papers by Moharam, Gaylord and anything on Rigorous Coupled Wave Analysis (RCWA), for example: [http://www.opticsinfobase.org/josa/abst ... m?id=58041](http://www.opticsinfobase.org/josa/abstract.cfm?id=58041)

posts.content_md:
Just curious, what does an e-beam master at 200 nm resolution cost per square cm?

PS. as far as I know Zebra doesn't calculate/record fringes directly, their method is really more akin to an advanced dot matrix method relying on interference to form the fringes. posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** Just curious, what does an e-beam master at 200 nm resolution cost per square cm?

Insofar as embossed holography is concerned, it depends on the quantity. However, I believe it's not that much since e-beams are fairly common and the equipment can be rented out. This is not the same as actually buying an e-beam machine. That's probably quite a bit. At ABNH, we had talked of moving into e-beam holography when I was there in the mid-90's. At that time, we discussed the pros and cons of renting out e-beam time or actually buying an e-beam in-house. To the best of my memory, buying one in the mid-90's, we were quoted in the hundreds of thousands. Now, some 15 years later, the price may well have gone down.

> **PinkysBrain:** To directly record fringes near <1/2 visible wavelengths e-beam seems to be the only game in town,

Not so. Cymer ( [http://www.cymer.com/](http://www.cymer.com/) ), here in San Diego provides lasers to the electronic industry for nanometer tracks on circuit boards. MIT's holo-video uses acousto-optics to create momentary Bragg planes in a crystal.

You don't have to record near < lambda/2 because the spatial frequency deos not have to be lambda/(2*n). This is the spatial frequency of two collimated beams hitting the plate from opposite sides of the film on-axis. Most glass masters for embossing are usually about 1000 l/mm, mostly because the response function for resist drops rapidly at about 1500 l/mm. However, 1000 l/mm creates fringes with a 1 micron separation. For recording CGH's with, say the Binary Detour Phase methods, a laser can be used.

posts.author: PinkysBrain
posts.content_md:
> **HoloM:** So my question was intended to search for some methods, which can be done in a home lab, with which I could proove my calculations of fringes or diffractive pixels are correct, or even to see the results as a real hologram. One thing I did in the last half year was to strip down a standard beamer to only have the DMD-Device for some experiments. There I have a working one now. Quite nice, as I simulated the signals of the color wheel with a microcontroller, in order to have a cheap really vibration free DMD-System.

The modulation is the easy part, the projection optics to get it down to a submicron resolution image to record is the hard part (you need a translation stage too of course, but precision there is less critical ... fringes not matching up exactly between recorded squares aren't going to ruin the hologram completely). Long working distance objectives might be able to be abused for something like this ... or the optics out of an old stepper if you can find one.

The Japanese seem to be the only ones doing much research into fringe printers, their early attempts were basically laser plotters ... but they have moved up, first to LCD projection fringe printers, presented at ISDH 2009 (I don't have the paper, but some people here probably do).

[http://river-valley.tv/development-of-f ... lications/](http://river-valley.tv/development-of-fringe-printer-and-its-practical-applications/)

> Also I found not very much about the principle zebra, geola and Rabbitholes use for printing their holograms.

As far as I know they all have a pixelized structure and are reconstructed with wide spectrum light sources, which is a pretty strong indication they use something like described in this thesis :

[http://arxiv.org/pdf/0902.0551](http://arxiv.org/pdf/0902.0551)

The people who wrote the ISDH paper mentioned above have now also abandoned fringe printing to use a very similar method. The main attraction is that you can record volume holograms, to get away from needing very narrow bandwidth light sources for reconstruction.

[http://spiedigitallibrary.org/proceedin ... 1/82810N_1](http://spiedigitallibrary.org/proceedings/resource/2/psisdg/8281/1/82810N_1)

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** There is even open source code :http://www.laser.ee.kansai-u.ac.jp/WaveFieldTools/

Not being able to read the Japanese, I was wondering if they had a way to determine angular spread and dispersion of the final image.

I was told by someone in Zebra (I believe it was Craig) that they were able to extract the 3D data set directly from a 3D software database, ie the polygon and vertex information of the 3D image, and then do a fringe calculation. I had myself thought of doing this sometime around 2000 but it occurred to me back then that a real display hologram has some dispersion, which gives it the hue and saturation - basically the colour spread of a hologram actually shot with a laser(s). The "back-calculation" of a hologram from vertex/polygon data does not have explicit colour, since the colour of a CGI is determined by the lighting superimposed on the object by lighting elements in the software. So, my question to myself was: How to determine the colour of the final hologram, if, in the "real world", these colours are produced by spurious reflections from the laser, the angle(s) at which the object beam hits the object(s), the bandwidth of the medium and the processing methods. As far as I could determine, you'd have to impose a specific wavelength and a specific bandwidth to every polygon in the mesh! In addition, you'd have to artificially insert an assumed spread of the "object beam" as it hits the "object", and then have either a multitude of vectors on ever polygon instead of just one normal vector, or to have curved polygons whose curvature would depend on the (assumed) object beam divergence. As far as I could see, that meant dealing with the entire data set using tensors instead of vectors to determine light reflection from the polygons! This seemd to be an overwhelming task, so I gave up on it for the time. As a friend of mine says: "That's project number 323!" The point of all this being, how does the software you referenced deal with the colour and beam divergence issue, assuming that it does?

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
In response to where one can get the e-beam done, when I worked at CFC/Northern Banknote we used a place in Russia, ostensibly because they were the cheapest, even though they were halfway around the world. What that price was, I don’t know, but check out their work at: [http://www.computer-holography.com/home.htm](http://www.computer-holography.com/home.htm). And I did see an actual embossed sample of the Salvador Dali image shown on their page, although it’s flat.

Another venue for those who really would like to dabble in e-beam holography would be to hook up with a university’s Electrical or Electronic engineering Department. While working at CFC, I made a trip up to the University of Wisconsin at Madison, (home of the Onion, America’s finest news source, [http://theonion.com](http://theonion.com), and once the residence of R. W. Wood) to visit the lab of some professor (I forgot their name, it was about 10 years ago or more, and it’s best that they remain nameless as you read on) who had a home made e-beam machine. It was an old electron microscope for the writer, and it was controlled by a PDP-11 computer! They used it to write resist for micro-circuits, and it was hoped that they could write e-beam holos for us.

However, their ancient device choked on our test pattern, too big of a file for their old PDP’s compiler, so it never went further than us donating to the research of nameless. But larger schools, like where my son goes at the U of I in Champaign, do have those devices. Maybe if you rattled the right cage you could find an understanding professor to grad student who would like to try out this type of project!

Or if you can find a junker of an SEM…

> **Dinesh:** Not being able to read the Japanese, I was wondering if they had a way to determine angular spread and dispersion of the final image.

I was talking about fringe printing in the part you quoted ... fringe printing is for thin holograms ... only suitable for rainbow holograms and holograms reconstructed with near monochromatic light sources.

As for volume CGHs ala Zebra/Rabbithole/etc ... I assume that what you do is you simply ignore the fact the volume hologram will have crosstalk and won't be purely wavelength selective on replay with a white light source (just like you do in analogue colour holography) and record R,G and B separately and hope for the best. You record using the method described in the thesis, you determine the hemispherical light field for each "hogel" which results from the synthetic light sources in the scene and record it, for R, G and B ... there is no synthetic equivalent of the object beam in this method (good riddance).

> I had myself thought of doing this sometime around 2000 but it occurred to me back then that a real display hologram has some dispersion, which gives it the hue and saturation

The dispersion is just distortion, nothing more.

> The "back-calculation" of a hologram from vertex/polygon data does not have explicit colour, since the colour of a CGI is determined by the lighting superimposed on the object by lighting elements in the software.

All the different colours and geometry in the scene contribute to a trichromatic 4D light field at the hologram plane, it's that light field which you record in analogue (strictly speaking you record trichromatic 2D light fields for a lot of points on a grid, but comes down to the same thing).

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** The dispersion is just distortion, nothing more.

Well, it depends on what you mean by "distortion". Dispersion is not an aberration, such as coma or astigmatism. It's dispersion that allows you to see the hologram, if the hologram had no dispersion, the bandwidth would be too thin to register on the retina. Colour is generally a dispersion effect, where the degree of dispersion gives the saturation (the hue being given by the centre frequency). So, if the diffraction from the hologram were to center around, say, 500nm +/- 10 nm, then the hologram would appear to be a "sharp" green. With no dispersion, the hologram would diffract at 500 +/- 0nm, which is impossible (it violates theTime-Energy uncertainy, since a single frequency means you measure an effect that occurs over a zero time interval))

> **PinkysBrain:** (strictly speaking you record trichromatic 2D light fields for a lot of points on a grid, but comes down to the same thing

Only in a photograph. In a hologram, you're recording phase information relative to the reference beam, so you're recording the magnitude of the E field (the intensity), the angle between the E field of the Object and the E field of the referene beams (the phase) and the separation of the peaks of the E field over a period of time (the frequency). You can think of this as a three dimensional phase diagram (here, "phase" refers to the system state, as opposed the optical phase). To make the recording possible, the E field across the entire aperture must be constant and stay constant over the period of the exposure, but this is not really a phase state, as much as it's an "existence condition" or "existence theorem".

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** It's unwanted and adds nothing useful to the image on replay ... the extra brightness you get from accepting a wider spectrum is wanted of course, but not the dispersion.

Colour is not brightness. The point is that without hue and chroma there is no hologram. Brightness is defined as the luminance is any given wavelength range for grey scale or for tristumulus values. There is no "increase" in brightness from a "wider spectrum" (you mean presumably a larger bandwidth rather than a wider spectrum, since our eyes cannot see a wider spectrum beyond, roughly 400nm to 700nm). The sum total of intensity is also different from the concept of brightness, since now you need to take into account the scotopic and photopic response functions. Without any colour, the image would simply be a greyscale, like an open-aperture "achromat" transmission. I would suggest that there's a difference between colour, the variation of colour and the tonal range of any given colour. All three of these are dispersive effects and encompass a given definition of delta lambda, but tonal range is a function of the integral of the photopic (or scotopic) function over lambda.

> **PinkysBrain:** I can see laser light just fine ... energy is important, not bandwidth.

Actually, you can't see laser light. In fact, you can't see any light at all! What you see is an interaction of light with matter that produces a visual stimulation. If, and when, you "see" a laser beam across a room, what you're seeing is the light reflected from dust. If there was no dust, you'd not see the beam. Certainly deep space is not permeated by an infinite amount of light a la Olber's Paradox. 

Again, the bandwidth defines energy. Without bandwidth there is no energy! The energy in any electromagnetic field is the integral of the energy density function over the wavelength. If you allow an "S" for an integral sign, then:

E = S<E(lambda)d(lambda)>

You have to put in the limits over the bandwidth from lambda(1) to lambda(2). However, without bandwidth

 lambda(1) = lambda(2)

and so

E = 0!

Also, laser light does have a bandwidth. You cannot have zero bandwidth! Consider what is meant by an item of physical reality outside of the purview of the EPR paper. In order to determine the objective reality of a phenomenon, you need to take a measurement, since, without a meausrement there is no physical reality. However, in order to measure something, you need to use a measuring instrument. However, all physical measuring systems have an inherent uncertainty. So, all measurements have an inherent uncertainty. So, in order to measure the speed of a car, you need to track the car over a specified distance and time it over a specific period. If the distance moved or the time interval is shorter than the uncertainty in measurement, then the physical reality of the car actaully moving is brought intop question. If you were measuring a frequency phenomenon, you need to time at least one complete period of the phenomenon. But, if the frequency is a Dirac delta - no bandwidth, then you would have to measure this frequency over zero time. In order to measure the frequency, you'd have to employ the Shannon criterion. But, measuring something over a zero period imlpies infinite uncertainty.

> **PinkysBrain:** Fortunately we have a trichromatic vision system and you can fake colours with RGB

Not faked. We takle advantage of the metamerism.

> **PinkysBrain:** The RGB colour system is what we rely on to create colour in a colour hologram ... the dispersion is just distortion.

All reflection holograms are coloured, it's just that the colour consists of a relatively small range. Usually, 

delat lambda < 50nm

However, the hologram is still dispersive to within 50nm. If delta lambda is greater, then we call it a "colour" hologram, but simply because the eye perceives more than one "colour" in the Newtonian scheme. 

Also, "distortion" is defined as the aberrations of an image. Bandwidth is not an aberration, not a Seidel aberrationn anyway. So a definition of distortion is needed.

> **PinkysBrain:** That's just an artifact of the recording process, what we aim to record/replay in a display hologram is the 4D light field coming from the object at the hologram plane (which Zebra et al do by recording lots of 2D light fields on a grid, as described in the thesis I linked).

4D light field? What are the 4 dimensions? As far as I'm aware, the hologram records phase and intensity, and variations thereof. A light field is a time and space variation of an electro-magnetic field.

 It's not what Zebra does.

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Dinesh - 

The "light field" is a construct utilized in a hot field of computer graphics / optics. 4D is just referring to a particular parameterization of rays that go through a 3-D scene (see, "plenoptic function.") You're probably already up to speed on this stuff, but one 4-D parameterization considers each ray as passing through two 2-D reference planes. If one plane has axes (u,v) and the other (s,t), then the properties of a ray through the volume is described by 4 position components: L(s,t,u,v).

Anyway, if this isn't something you've read about I think you'll get a kick out of it. Light field-thinking has generated some neat advances in computational photography.

[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_field](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_field) (re: 4D)

[http://graphics.stanford.edu/~levoy/research.html](http://graphics.stanford.edu/~levoy/research.html) (Levoy's lightfield stuff)

[http://cameraculture.media.mit.edu/](http://cameraculture.media.mit.edu/) Ramesh Raskar's stuff

By the way, re: Zebra, my understanding was that, no, fringes are not computed. An object beam (pencil?) is composed of what a scene looks like at various angles through a particular hogel, and a reference beam interferes with it to make the fringes. Of course, from a background of physics, the field variables are independant of the dimensionality of the space, except when your working with phase space, so I thought Pinky's Brain was talking about phase space. 

I'm pretty sure that Zebra does not use a dot matrix. There are two reasons for this. One is that I was the first person to use a Dot Matrix machine, to the best of my belief. Ken Harris designed and built the first one and sold it to ABNH around 1994. At that time I was assigned to be the dot matrix operator so I had the (unenviable!) task of debugging that first machine. However, Mike was using his technique at MIT before 1994. Secondly, a dot marix relies on a set of "quantised dots" and the Zebra holograms are continuous. 

One thing that does confuse me is the use of the word "hogel". As I understand it, a hogel is a 3 dimensional image element. As such, it needs three numbers to determine the size. Another point is that I know that they take a ray from the scene from various angles, but how do they determine the direction of the ray? It must be computational. posts.author: PinkysBrain
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** I'm pretty sure that Zebra does not use a dot matrix. There are two reasons for this. One is that I was the first person to use a Dot Matrix machine, to the best of my belief. Ken Harris designed and built the first one and sold it to ABNH around 1994. At that time I was assigned to be the dot matrix operator so I had the (unenviable!) task of debugging that first machine. However, Mike was using his technique at MIT before 1994. Secondly, a dot marix relies on a set of "quantised dots" and the Zebra holograms are continuous.

The appearance of continuity in a discretized image is just a question of resolution ... also traditional dot matrix interferes a couple of beams, the object beam is not generally a highly converging beam modulated with a hemisphere intensity pattern appropriate for the dot.

It's dot matrix on steroids.

> Surely this is a contradiction? Another point is that I know that they take a ray from the scene from various angles, but how do they determine the direction of the ray?

The virtual hologram is simply a window in the synthetic 3D scene, pick a spot on it, any spot ... at that spot they need to ray trace in all directions of a hemisphere (if you want real images in front of the hologram plane you have to start the rays behind the hologram plane and trace towards and through it). Then add some discretization.

They don't pick the direction, they take them all. Every ray on the hemisphere represents one pixel on the SLM you use to modulate the object beam for the hogel.
